questions.question: A developer is building an ASP.NET Core web app that must run on Linux containers in Azure with automatic HTTPS, deployment slots and integrated authentication. Which compute service should they choose?
options: Azure Virtual Machines with a custom Linux image
Azure Service Fabric stateless service cluster
Azure Batch with a low-priority node pool and autoscale
Azure App Service for Linux with deployment slots
questions.explanation: Azure App Service is a fully managed PaaS that natively supports Linux containers, custom domains with free TLS certificates, deployment slots for staging/production swaps and built-in authentication via Easy Auth. Virtual Machines would require manual setup of TLS, slot-equivalent swaps and identity middleware. Batch is purpose-built for parallel HPC and rendering workloads, not long-running web servers — autoscale alone does not turn it into a web platform. Service Fabric runs microservices clusters but lacks native slot swaps and Easy Auth integration.

questions.question: An application stores millions of small JSON documents that must be queried by partition key with single-digit-millisecond latency at global scale. Which Azure service is BEST suited?
options: Azure Table Storage with geo-redundant replication
Azure Cache for Redis with AOF persistence enabled
Azure Cosmos DB using the NoSQL (Core) API
Azure SQL Database with read replicas in two regions
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed multi-model database that guarantees single-digit-millisecond reads and writes and 99.999% availability across regions. The NoSQL (Core) API is ideal for JSON documents queried by partition key. Table Storage is cheaper but caps latency SLAs at 10 ms and has no multi-region writes. Azure SQL is relational — read replicas help reads but not key-lookup latency at scale. Redis is a volatile cache, not durable primary storage even with persistence.

questions.question: Which Cosmos DB consistency level provides the strongest consistency while still allowing multi-region writes?
options: The bounded staleness consistency level
The eventual consistency level only
The session consistency level by default
The strong consistency level globally
questions.explanation: Strong consistency in Cosmos DB is incompatible with multi-region writes — it requires a single write region. Bounded staleness is the strongest level that supports multi-region writes: reads lag behind writes by at most K versions or T time. Session is the default and only guarantees read-your-writes within a single client session. Eventual provides the weakest guarantees and offers no ordering.

questions.question: A developer wants an Azure Function to run on the first day of every month at 03:00 UTC. Which trigger and configuration should they use?
options: Timer trigger with NCRONTAB expression "0 0 3 1 * *"
Queue trigger fed by a Logic App scheduled action
Event Grid trigger filtered to a monthly system event
HTTP trigger invoked by an external cron scheduler service
questions.explanation: Azure Functions Timer triggers use a 6-field NCRONTAB syntax: {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}. "0 0 3 1 * *" means second=0, minute=0, hour=3, day-of-month=1, every month, any day-of-week — exactly the first day of every month at 03:00 UTC. A queue or HTTP trigger driven by an external scheduler adds an external dependency and a single point of failure. Event Grid does not emit a calendar-based system event tied to month boundaries.

questions.question: An Azure Function on the Consumption plan must process up to 5,000 messages per second from Service Bus, but you observe scale-out is too slow. Which plan should you switch to for predictable, faster scale and no cold starts?
options: Premium plan with pre-warmed instance pools
Container Apps with KEDA event-driven scaling
Dedicated (App Service) plan with autoscale rules
Free Consumption tier with extended timeouts
questions.explanation: Functions Premium plan provides pre-warmed instances (no cold start), VNet integration and faster event-driven scale-out than Consumption while still billing per execution. Dedicated (App Service) plan does not scale automatically on event volume — it requires manual or metric-based autoscale rules that lag behind queue bursts. Container Apps is a separate product, not a Functions hosting plan. There is no Free tier for Azure Functions.

questions.question: Which Azure Storage service should be used to host static website assets (HTML, CSS, JS) directly served from a custom domain over HTTPS at the lowest cost?
options: Azure Table Storage with row-key partitioning by URL path
Azure Files SMB share mounted by the web tier for content
Azure Queue Storage configured for browser read-only access
Azure Blob Storage with the Static website feature on $web
questions.explanation: Blob Storage has a Static website feature that exposes the $web container at a primary endpoint, supports custom domains and CDN/Front Door for HTTPS termination — the cheapest way to host SPAs and static sites. Azure Files exposes SMB/NFS shares for application data — it is not an HTTPS web origin. Queue Storage stores messages, not browsable files. Table Storage stores key-value rows and cannot serve arbitrary content over HTTP.

questions.question: A developer must grant a web app running on App Service permission to read secrets from Azure Key Vault WITHOUT storing any credentials in code or config. Which approach is correct?
options: Use a service principal whose client secret is committed to the repo
Store the Key Vault primary access key in an App Service app setting
Enable a system-assigned managed identity granted Key Vault Get
Embed a long-lived SAS token in the application source code itself
questions.explanation: Managed identities provide an automatically rotated Azure AD identity to Azure resources. The App Service uses this identity to authenticate to Key Vault — no credentials in code or configuration. After enabling the system-assigned identity, grant it Get on secrets via access policies or RBAC. Each of the other options stores a long-lived credential somewhere reachable from source or a portal setting, which violates the requirement.

questions.question: An application needs to receive a notification within seconds when a new blob is uploaded to a container, with built-in filtering on file extension. Which Azure service provides the BEST event delivery?
options: Event Grid subscription on the storage account with a suffix filter
A timer-driven Function polling the container every 30 seconds for changes
Service Bus topic with a SQL filter that is populated by the uploader
Azure Storage Queue written by a custom uploader for each new blob
questions.explanation: Azure Event Grid natively integrates with Storage and pushes Blob Created events with subject prefix and suffix filters (for example, subject ending in .jpg), giving low-latency server-push notifications. Polling is wasteful and adds latency up to the poll interval. Service Bus topics are not connected to Storage events out of the box — they only fire if the uploader publishes a message. A custom uploader writing to a Storage Queue couples producers to consumers and breaks when files arrive via tools that bypass the uploader.

questions.question: Which Azure messaging service guarantees FIFO ordering AND duplicate detection within a configurable time window?
options: Event Hubs partitions with ordering by partition key
Event Grid topic with replay and subject ordering
Service Bus queue with sessions and duplicate detection
Storage Queue with poison retry and visibility timeout tuning
questions.explanation: Service Bus queues support sessions (ordered, FIFO delivery per session ID) and duplicate detection (rejects messages with the same MessageId within a 20-second to 7-day window). Event Hubs preserves order per partition but has no built-in dedup. Event Grid is push-style event distribution with at-least-once delivery and no FIFO or dedup guarantees. Storage Queues offer only best-effort FIFO and provide no native deduplication.

questions.question: A web API protects endpoints with Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD). A daemon service running on a VM must call the API without any user interaction. Which OAuth 2.0 flow is appropriate?
options: Implicit flow with response_type set to token
Client Credentials flow with a certificate
Authorization Code flow with PKCE for SPAs
Device Code flow polling for user approval
questions.explanation: Client Credentials flow is designed for service-to-service and daemon scenarios with no user — the client authenticates with its own credentials (client ID + certificate or secret) to obtain an access token. Authorization Code with PKCE is for interactive end users in single-page or native apps. Implicit flow is deprecated and never appropriate for a confidential client. Device Code is for input-constrained user devices like TVs, not headless daemons.

questions.question: Which Microsoft Graph permission type should a multi-tenant SaaS app request to read user mail on behalf of the signed-in user?
options: Application permission Directory.AccessAsUser.All
Delegated permission Mail.Read with user consent
Application permission Mail.Read with admin consent
App-only permission Mail.ReadWrite.All tenant-wide
questions.explanation: Delegated permissions act on behalf of the signed-in user and are scoped to that user's mailbox. Mail.Read (delegated) is the least-privileged scope that satisfies the requirement. Application permissions are app-only (no user) and access every mailbox in the tenant — over-broad here and requiring tenant-admin consent. Directory.AccessAsUser.All targets the directory, not mail. Mail.ReadWrite.All adds write permission that is not needed.

questions.question: A developer wants to deliver a dynamic web app globally with low latency, automatic HTTPS, custom domains and a managed CDN — without provisioning a CDN profile manually. Which option is BEST?
options: Application Gateway v2 with autoscale enabled
Azure Front Door (Standard or Premium) profile
Traffic Manager profile using priority routing
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft premium tier
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global Layer-7 load balancer with built-in CDN caching, WAF, automatic HTTPS via managed certificates and split-TCP for low TTFB on dynamic content. Azure CDN profiles cache static content but do not load-balance dynamic origins across regions on their own. Traffic Manager is DNS-based steering only — it does not terminate TLS or cache. Application Gateway is regional, so it cannot deliver low latency globally without per-region deployment.

questions.question: Which Azure App Configuration feature lets a developer roll out a new feature to 10% of users and progressively increase the rollout WITHOUT redeploying the app?
options: Managed identities bound to the App Service plan
Configuration snapshots pinned to a named release tag
Key-value pairs scoped by labels per environment
Feature flags with a Targeting filter for rollout
questions.explanation: App Configuration feature flags support filters: Targeting (percentage rollout, user/group lists), Time Window and Custom. The Targeting filter lets you specify a default rollout percentage and per-group overrides without code changes — the client reads the new value at refresh time. Labels organize config across environments but do not toggle features. Snapshots are immutable point-in-time copies for rollback, not progressive delivery. Managed identities solve authentication, not feature exposure.

questions.question: An ARM template deployment must reference a secret stored in Key Vault at deployment time without exposing the value in deployment logs. Which technique is correct?
options: Use the @description() function on a parameter named for the secret
Hard-code the secret value in the parameters file and gitignore the file
Reference the secret in the parameters file via keyVault and secretName
Pass the secret as a query-string parameter on the deployment script URL
questions.explanation: ARM and Bicep deployments can dereference Key Vault secrets directly in the parameters file using a reference object: { "reference": { "keyVault": { "id": "..." }, "secretName": "..." } }. Azure Resource Manager fetches the secret at deploy time and never writes the value to deployment logs. @description() is for parameter documentation only and has no impact on secret retrieval. Hard-coding or passing the value via query string places the plaintext into source, history or telemetry.

questions.question: Which API Management policy should be used to throttle a specific subscription to 1,000 calls per minute?
options: <rate-limit calls="1000" renewal-period="60" />
<quota calls="1000" renewal-period="3600" />
<set-backend-service base-url="https://api.example.com" />
<cors><allowed-origins>*</allowed-origins></cors>
questions.explanation: rate-limit (and rate-limit-by-key) enforce short-window per-subscription throttling — calls per renewal-period in seconds. quota is for longer-term volume caps such as per hour, per day or per month and rejects only once the cap is exhausted in that window. set-backend-service rewrites the upstream URL and has nothing to do with throttling. cors configures CORS preflight handling. For 1,000 calls per minute, rate-limit with calls=1000 and renewal-period=60 is the correct policy.

questions.question: A developer wants to monitor an Azure Function with distributed tracing, exception capture and live metrics. Which service should they integrate?
options: Azure Monitor Logs only, with custom Kusto alert rules
Azure Service Health combined with resource health probes
Network Watcher packet capture on the function host plan
Application Insights with auto-instrumentation enabled
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the APM service for Azure apps — it captures requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces across services with correlation IDs (distributed tracing) and offers Live Metrics and Smart Detection. Azure Monitor Logs is the underlying log store; on its own it lacks APM correlation and live metrics. Service Health reports Azure platform incidents that affect a subscription, not application-level telemetry. Network Watcher inspects packets and routes, not function-level traces.

questions.question: Which Application Insights query language is used in the Logs blade to search telemetry?
options: T-SQL routed through the Azure SQL Database connector
Lucene query strings shared with Cognitive Search
Kusto Query Language (KQL) via Azure Data Explorer
GraphQL queries against the Azure Monitor schema
questions.explanation: Application Insights and Azure Monitor Logs use Kusto Query Language (KQL), the same query language as Azure Data Explorer. Example: requests | where timestamp > ago(1h) | summarize count() by resultCode. T-SQL is for Azure SQL Database, not Monitor. Lucene powers some search engines (including Azure Cognitive Search) but is not the query language for Monitor. GraphQL is not a Monitor query interface.

questions.question: Which Azure Container Apps feature is BEST suited to scale a service to zero when idle and back up on incoming HTTP traffic?
options: Azure VM Scale Set integration provisioned in Bicep
Dapr sidecar with pub/sub and state-store bindings
KEDA-based scale rule using the HTTP scaler
Manual scale rule pinned to a fixed replica count
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps uses KEDA under the hood. The HTTP scaler scales 0→N based on concurrent request volume per replica, including scale-to-zero when traffic stops. Dapr provides service-to-service primitives like pub/sub and state — it is orthogonal to scaling. Manual replica counts cannot reach zero on idle. VM Scale Sets are a different compute product and are not used to scale Container Apps replicas.

questions.question: A developer needs to generate a time-limited URL that grants read-only access to a single blob without sharing the storage account key. Which feature should they use?
options: Anonymous public container access on the blob endpoint
User delegation SAS or service SAS scoped to the blob
Stored access policy attached to a queue at account scope
Account-level shared access signature for the storage account
questions.explanation: A service SAS — or, preferably, a user delegation SAS signed by Entra ID credentials — targets a specific blob with read-only permission and an expiry. The user delegation form does not require the account key at all. An account-level SAS grants access across services and is broader than needed. Anonymous public access removes authentication entirely. A stored access policy on a queue applies to queues, not blobs.

questions.question: Which Azure Cognitive Search feature lets a developer surface results enriched with AI-generated metadata (e.g., key phrases, OCR text) extracted from PDFs and images?
options: Skillsets and indexers running cognitive enrichment
Synonym maps that alias query terms at search time
Suggesters that power as-you-type autocomplete entries
Scoring profiles that re-rank results by field weighting
questions.explanation: Skillsets attach AI skills (OCR, key phrase extraction, entity recognition, custom Web API skills) to an indexer pipeline, projecting enriched fields into the search index. Suggesters drive autocomplete from existing index fields but cannot extract new metadata. Scoring profiles tune relevance weighting at query time without adding new fields. Synonym maps rewrite query terms with alternate forms — they neither read documents nor produce new content.
